You say since when, for how long, how long ago and how soon something happens (da, fa, per, tra / fra, in, entro, durante, mentre).
I've been living in Florence for two years.
I worked in Sibiu for six months.
She made the blanket in two days.
To say since when / for how long something has been going on with DA + present: Abito qui da due anni.
To say how long ago something happened with FA: due anni fa.
To say how long a finished action lasted with PER: Ho lavorato lì per sei mesi.
To say how soon with TRA / FRA and how long it takes with IN.
To use entro, durante and mentre.
To describe a visit to the doctor and a long journey.
Florence, 12th November. Giulia and Matei are at the surgery of Dr Ricci, the gynaecologist, for the first scan.
Good morning. So, Mrs Esposito, how long have you known you're pregnant?
For about a month. I did the test on the fourteenth of October.
And when did you last have a gynaecological check-up?
A year ago, in Naples. Before the wedding.
Yes, for six weeks now. But it's been a bit better for a few days.
Excuse me, doctor, and when will it pass?
Usually in two or three weeks. Right, let's have a look… There. Can you see it? And this is the heart.
That's normal. It's been beating for about three weeks. The due date is the twentieth of May.
The twentieth? Like our wedding, the twentieth of September!
Do you want to know if it's a boy or a girl? I'll be able to tell you in eight weeks.
No, thank you. We want a surprise. We decided three days ago, after two hours of discussion.
Good. Then I'll see you in a month. And Mr Popa, sit down: you've been as white as a sheet for five minutes.
sheet ("bianco come un lenzuolo" = as white as a sheet)
Stress on "FEE": e-ko-gra-FEE-a, with "i-a" in separate syllables.
The diphthong "uo" run together: len-TSWO-lo. Z = "ts".
O and I separate: ko-een-chee-DEN-tsa. CI = "chee".
1. DA + present: since when, for how long
For an action that began in the past and is STILL GOING ON, Italian uses the PRESENT + DA (where English uses "have been… for / since"):
I've been living here for two years.
We've known each other for three years.
Don't use the passato prossimo: "Abito qui da due anni", NOT "Ho abitato qui da due anni" (the typical mistake of English speakers, who think of "I have lived").
DA + a length of time (da due anni) or DA + a point in time (dal 2020, da lunedì, da quando ero piccolo).
"Fa" goes AFTER the time expression and is used with a past tense:
A year ago I was in Naples.
It works just like English "ago": "due anni FA", NOT "fa due anni".
3. PER: how long it lasted (a finished action)
For a finished length of time, with the passato prossimo, use PER (or no preposition). Compare with DA:
Ho lavorato a Sibiu per sei mesi.
Lavoro a Firenze da tre anni.
Ho studiato l’italiano per un anno.
Trick: if it's over, use PER. If it has been going on and still is ("I have been… for"), use DA.
4. TRA / FRA and IN: in how long, how long it takes
in (how long it takes to do something)
Ha fatto la coperta in due giorni.
"Tra" and "fra" mean exactly the same. You choose by sound: "fra tre giorni" (not "tra tre"), "tra fratelli" (not "fra fratelli").
"Tra un’ora" = in an hour's time (that's when it starts). "In un’ora" = within an hour (that's how long it takes). DON'T mix them up!
Durante il viaggio ha lavorato a maglia.
Mentre Ion dormiva, Doina lavorava a maglia.
NOT "durante viaggiava" and NOT "mentre il viaggio". Durante + noun, mentre + verb.
I have to finish by Friday.
While Ion was sleeping, Doina was reading.
"I've been studying Italian for a year." (and still am)
Ho studiato l’italiano da un anno.

Ion Popa had been working for the railways for forty years when he retired, two years ago. In his whole life he had taken a plane only once, in 1994, for a conference in Warsaw, and ever since he had told everyone: "Never again. Man is made for rails, not for clouds."

So when Doina decided to go to Florence to see her pregnant daughter-in-law, Ion planned a route by train. Sibiu, Budapest, Vienna, Venice, Florence: four trains, three connections, twenty-six hours of travel. Doina protested for three days. Then she bought six balls of white wool and said: "All right. But during the journey I'm knitting, and you're not talking about locomotives."

They left on a Tuesday morning at six. While the train crossed the Hungarian plain, Doina knitted and Ion looked out of the window with the expression of a child in a toy shop. Every so often he would say: "They electrified this line in 1978," then remember his promise and fall silent.

In Vienna they had a two-hour wait. Ion spent the whole time studying the departures board, the way another man would study a painting in a museum. Doina, meanwhile, had already finished the first ball of wool. The night train to Venice left on time, at nine in the evening. Ion slept like a baby for eight hours. Doina, on the other hand, hardly slept at all, because the man in the next bunk snored like a steam engine. At three in the morning Doina finished the second ball of wool and started the third, while the man next door kept on snoring.

They arrived in Florence, at Santa Maria Novella station, on Wednesday at eight in the evening, ten minutes late. Ion was offended: "In Romania ten minutes isn't late. But here in Italy I expected better." Matei and Giulia had been waiting on the platform for half an hour. Doina hugged Giulia and immediately put a parcel in her hands: a small white blanket, ever so soft, made in twenty-six hours.

They stayed in Florence for a week. Doina spent almost all her time in Graziella's kitchen. The two women had no language in common, but after three days they understood each other perfectly: Graziella taught her ribollita, Doina taught her sarmale, and both of them taught Pietro not to steal dough from the bowl. Without success. Pietro, on the other hand, learned to say "noroc" in one afternoon.

Ion, for his part, found a friend. Signor Franco had been a stationmaster in Florence for thirty-five years, from 1960 to 1995. Every morning the two men sat in the station bar, drank a coffee and watched the trains. They didn't speak the same language, but they talked about locomotives, and for locomotives, it seems, you don't need any language.

On the second-to-last day Matei took his parents to the workshop. Bellini was waiting for them at the door, in a jacket and tie. He showed Doina the portrait of the woman with the blue veil, which had come back from Sibiu a month earlier to be photographed. Doina stood in front of the painting for ten minutes without saying anything. Then she said in Romanian: "Mum, in six months you'll be a great-grandmother." Bellini didn't understand the words, but he understood everything else.

On the last evening, at dinner at Graziella's, Ion stood up. He took out of his pocket an old silver pocket watch, with a little locomotive engraved on the lid. "They gave it to me forty years ago, on my first day at work," he said, and Matei translated. "Since then it has never lost a single minute. It's for the baby. That way it'll learn early that trains, and people, must be punctual."

Signor Franco raised his glass. "To the baby," he said. "And to trains that arrive on time. Even in Italy." Everyone laughed. Giulia took the watch and put it on the small white blanket, next to Ernesto's brush and the new one. The baby hadn't been born yet, and it already had three presents from three different generations.

The next morning, on the platform, Doina hugged Giulia for a long time. "We'll be back in six months," she said. "For the birth." "By plane this time?" Matei asked. Ion looked at him as if he had uttered a blasphemy. "By train," he replied. "Twenty-six hours. Your mother has already bought another ten balls of wool."
